name: Floodline Scavenger's Patched Coat Kit
description: The centerpiece is a long duster coat — originally a PolyRoute-brand weathershell, now unrecognizable under decades of repairs. The coat falls to mid-calf in dirty charcoal, its surface a topographic map of patches: waxed cotton over the shoulders, a square of recycled rubberized tarp at the left hip, strips of silver self-repair tape running along every seam like stitched scars. The lining has been partially removed and replaced with salvaged mylar emergency blanket material, giving it a faint crinkle with every movement and serious thermal retention. Beneath the coat: a ribbed tank in stained off-white tucked into high-waisted cargo pants in faded black denim so worn the knees are almost white, with a functional knee pad sewn into the right leg from a salvaged sports brace. Feet are wrapped in double wool socks visible above low-cut boots that have been resoled with a thick rubber compound and laced with paracord in mismatched colors — one strand bright red, one gray, a detail that in certain Shelf neighborhoods signals a specific salvage crew affiliation. A wide-brimmed hat in stiffened waxed canvas, darkened by rain and oil, sits low over the brow. The hat's band is wrapped with a strip of copper wire from which small salvaged objects hang — a cracked data chip, a single augmentation port cap, a flattened bottle cap embossed with a long-defunct street vendor's mark. Gene-compatible: the coat's back panel has been manually cut and re-hemmed to accommodate a prehensile tail, the edges finished with a whip-stitch of heavy nylon thread.
functionality: Mylar lining provides significant thermal retention in flooded industrial zones. Waxed patches and rubberized hip panel deflect acid rain splash. Knee pad integrated into trousers for crawling through collapsed infrastructure. Paracord lacing doubles as emergency cordage. Hat provides face and neck protection from overhead drip zones. Tail accommodation allows gene-modified wearers full mobility without coat damage.
what_it_says: A person who moves through flooded ruins and collapsed corridors regularly — not as a one-time emergency but as a daily routine. The hanging objects on the hat band are a personal archive, each one a relic of somewhere they've been or something they've survived. The paracord colors, if you know how to read them, tell you exactly who they run with.
manufacturer: Self-modified base coat (stripped PolyRoute), remaining components sourced from Shelf market stalls and personal salvage
price_range: Φ8–Φ25 in current parts; coat itself is years of accumulated labor
story_hooks: The cracked data chip hanging from the hat band isn't fully dead. A street tech with the right reader discovers it contains a partial map of a pre-flood sub-level that corponation surveyors have been quietly looking for.

The paracord color combination — red over gray — is the identifier of a salvage crew that was supposedly wiped out in a structural collapse eight months ago. Someone who knew that crew sees the boots and has questions.

The tail accommodation was added by someone else — the stitching is a different hand. The coat was inherited, and the original owner's last known location was somewhere the current wearer claims never to have been.
related_entities: Arcturus Defense Solutions ChemoShield BX-2 Dermal Toxin Barrier Implant

physical_description.visual_profile: A weathered, utilitarian silhouette of someone who lives at the margins—long duster coat worn like armor, layered with salvage and repair. The figure reads as perpetually ready to move, climb, or disappear into the urban decay. Despite the poverty signaled by every patch, there's an intentional, almost ritualistic care in how the repairs are arranged. The visible tail accommodation and mismatched boot laces suggest genetic modification acceptance and crew affiliation. The overall impression: capable survivor, not desperate victim.
physical_description.fit: Deliberately oversized and unrestricted—the coat hangs loose to facilitate movement and gear carrying, the cargo pants sit at natural waist for easy access to pockets, the tank undershirt is snug but practical. Every garment prioritizes function over form. The knee pad reinforces the right leg for climbing or kneeling work. Compression is absent; freedom of movement is the aesthetic.
physical_description.primary_material: Base coat: deteriorated synthetic weathershell (PolyRoute origin, now nearly unidentifiable). Patches: waxed cotton, recycled rubberized tarp, self-repair tape. Lining: salvaged mylar emergency blanket. Pants: faded black denim, heavily worn. Tank: cotton blend ribbing. Hat: stiffened waxed canvas. Boots: resoled with industrial rubber compound.
physical_description.texture: Visibly tactile and varied—smooth self-repair tape against rough waxed cotton patches, the faint crinkle of mylar with movement, weathered canvas hat with oil-darkened surface, worn denim soft and thin at stress points, heavy nylon whip-stitch visible on tail panel, paracord laces with frayed ends. Overall: rough, well-used, unpolished.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant palette: dirty charcoal (coat), faded black (pants), stained off-white (tank). Accents: silver self-repair tape running as 'scars' along seams, bright red paracord (right boot), gray paracord (left boot), copper wire band on hat brim catching light. The color scheme reads as functionally monochromatic with intentional accent colors that signal crew affiliation.
physical_description.closures: Coat: likely standard zippers heavily patched over, possibly some friction-fitted panels where zippers have failed. Pants: traditional button/zip fly, reinforced at stress points. Tank: none (pull-over). Hat: none (fitted). Boots: paracord lacing (mismatched colors), tight enough to be secure. No magnetic snaps or modern tech closures—everything is mechanical and repairable.
distinctive_features: Topographic map of patch work across entire coat surface—each repair tells a story of survival
Mylar emergency blanket lining visible when coat moves—functional insulation and light-reflective property
Back panel cut and re-hemmed to accommodate prehensile tail (heavy nylon whip-stitch finishing)
Silver self-repair tape runs along every seam like stitched scars—both practical and aesthetic
Recycled rubberized tarp patch at left hip—waterproofing for specific wear area
Waxed cotton shoulder panels—reinforced against carrying weight or friction
Knee pad on right leg from salvaged sports brace—climbing/crawling utility
Mismatched paracord boot laces (red and gray)—signals specific Shelf salvage crew affiliation
Hat band decorated with copper wire from which hang small salvaged objects: cracked data chip, augmentation port cap, flattened vendor bottle cap—personal trophies and lucky talismans
Visible double wool socks—warmth in ungoverned territories with poor infrastructure
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 / Sub-grade salvage tier—every element screams ungoverned zone dwelling. The coat has been worn through multiple lifecycle iterations. The absence of any branded logos (save the stripped PolyRoute origin now invisible under repairs), the deliberate, careful patchwork, and the salvaged components all signal someone operating outside formal economy. This is not poverty fashion; this is survival wear.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing this outfit identifies you as a Floodline scavenger—part of the salvage ecosystem that picks through the GLMZ's discarded infrastructure and failed corpo tech. The mismatched paracord laces signal crew affiliation and mutual recognition in the Shelf markets. The hat's copper wire trinkets suggest spiritual or superstitious attachment to salvaged history. The prehensile tail accommodation signals genetic modification acceptance in ungoverned spaces where augmentation is neither regulated nor judged. This person operates in the liminal spaces: flooded old industrial zones, abandoned megastructure basements, the gaps between Tier 1 corpo zones.
physical_description.condition_typical: Perpetually weathered and in active repair. The coat will never be 'clean'—dirt, rust stains, and water marks are permanent. Patches will fray at edges; new ones will be added regularly. The mylar lining will crinkle louder as it degrades. The boots will be re-resoled multiple times. The hat will darken further with rain and oil exposure. This is not a garment that deteriorates—it evolves. Each wear adds patina and story.

image_prompt: Neo-noir fashion photography: a lean figure in a long patched duster coat standing in a flooded concrete basement, knee-deep in murky water reflecting neon. The coat's patchwork of waxed cotton, tarp, and silver self-repair tape is backlit by a flickering blue-green industrial light source, casting shadows of the patches across grimy brick walls. The figure's wide-brimmed waxed canvas hat is pulled low, showing the copper wire band adorned with salvaged trinkets catching the neon glow. Paracord boot laces (one red, one gray) are visible above water level, secured to resoled industrial boots. The mylar lining crinkles audibly as the figure shifts, catching light like broken mirrors. The coat hangs loose and asymmetrical, the back panel visibly re-hemmed for a prehensile tail silhouette. Abandoned PolyRoute signage peels from the wall behind. Urban decay, survival, ungoverned zone aesthetic. Shot on dark mannequin or model with genetic modification prosthetics (tail suggestion). Moody, high contrast, dirty tungsten and neon lighting. --ar 2:3 --v 6
